A share card from a selection

Select a passage in the article. The card under it shows the passage, with its emphasis, in the largest type that fits. The card is an HTML figure styled with CSS and drawn by a canvas, so it can be saved, shared or copied as a PNG.

Commonplace books

A commonplace book is a notebook of passages copied out of other books. Readers have kept them for centuries, and the copying was the point: writing a sentence out by hand was a way to keep it.

John Locke published a method for indexing one, so that a passage copied years earlier could be found again by its subject. A quotation is only useful if it can be found.

Sharing a sentence from a web page is the same habit. The reader selects it and sends it to someone, usually as plain text and sometimes as a picture of the text.
Show the code the figure, the quote, the fit and the export
  1. The card is a figure inside a canvas.
  2. The canvas on the page.
  3. The three styles are CSS: gradients, background-clip: text, text-wrap: balance, shadows.
  4. The selection as a quote, with emphasis kept and everything else flattened.
  5. The largest type that fits, measured with scrollHeight on the figure.
  6. Draw the figure at the size of the picture.
  7. Make the PNG.
  8. Save, share and copy.

How it works

The figure is a drawable child of a canvas with layoutsubtree, so the browser lays it out and styles it like any element, and scrollHeight on it reports whether the quote fits. The figure is 600 by 315 CSS pixels for the link preview size. The canvas bitmap is 1200 by 630, and drawElementImage(figure, 0, 0, 1200, 630) draws the figure at twice its layout size. canvas.toBlob() gives the PNG. The selected text is copied with Range.cloneContents(), keeping em, strong and code and flattening everything else.

These start when you press the button. They build their own cards.

Findings

Measured in headless Chromium 157 on Linux with a software renderer, 2026-11-21.

  • A figure drawn larger than its layout is drawn again, not stretched. The check below draws a 1 px line at four times its size and finds hard edges. A card laid out at 600 px therefore exports at 1200 px with sharp type.
  • The canvas isn't tainted by same-origin element content: toBlob() returns a PNG of the requested size for all three formats.
  • Layout queries work on a canvas child. scrollHeight and clientHeight of the figure drive the type size, with no canvas text measuring.
  • The figure's layout box can be larger than the canvas element. The canvas is shown at the width of the page (about 396 px on a phone) while the figure is 600 px wide. The picture is complete, and the page doesn't scroll sideways because the stage clips.
  • The figure is inert. It is drawn at a different size from its layout, so its hit boxes would be in the wrong place. Nothing in it needs to be pressed.

Not verified: navigator.share() with a file and writing a PNG to the clipboard (the headless browser has neither a share sheet nor clipboard permission), and how the saved picture looks in a messaging app.
